job.style: a passage that starts from a common wrong idea and corrects it

passage: Many students believe that heavy objects fall faster than light ones, or that gravity is only a force between massive planets. However, the Universal Law of Gravitation states that every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force, regardless of their size. Even a small pen exerts a gravitational pull on a book nearby, though this force is too tiny to notice. When we drop objects in a vacuum, where air resistance is absent, a feather and a stone fall at exactly the same rate because acceleration due to gravity is independent of an object's mass. Furthermore, gravity does not simply vanish once you leave Earth's atmosphere; it continues to act on satellites and astronauts in space, keeping them in orbit. It is also a common mistake to think that mass and weight are identical. Mass is the constant amount of matter in a body, measured in kilograms, while weight is the force with which Earth pulls that body, measured in Newtons. Finally, remember that fluids exert pressure in all directions, not just downwards. Whether an object sinks or floats depends on the buoyant force relative to its weight, not just whether the object is heavy or light.

items.evidence: When we drop objects in a vacuum, where air resistance is absent, a feather and a stone fall at exactly the same rate because acceleration due to gravity is independent of an object's mass.
items.q: A heavy ball and a light ball are dropped together in a vacuum. What happens?
options: Both balls reach the ground together
The heavy ball reaches the ground first
The light ball reaches the ground first
Neither ball falls because there is no gravity
items.explain: In a vacuum, gravity gives every object the same acceleration, whatever its mass.

wrong.why: thinks air helps the lighter ball fall first
thinks there is no gravity in a vacuum

items.evidence: Even a small pen exerts a gravitational pull on a book nearby, though this force is too tiny to notice.
items.q: Why do we never see a pen and a book pulling each other?
options: Their pull on each other is too weak
Gravity acts only between planets and stars
Only the heavier object pulls the other
Air around them blocks the pull
items.explain: Every object pulls on others, but a pen's gravitational pull is too tiny to notice.

wrong.why: thinks gravity exists only between huge bodies
thinks only the bigger object attracts
thinks air stops gravity from acting

items.evidence: Furthermore, gravity does not simply vanish once you leave Earth's atmosphere; it continues to act on satellites and astronauts in space, keeping them in orbit.
items.q: What keeps a satellite circling Earth high above the air?
options: Earth's gravity still pulls on it up there
Gravity ends above the air, so air holds it
Gravity acts only between planets, not satellites
It is light, so it floats instead of falling
items.explain: Gravity does not vanish above the atmosphere; it keeps satellites in orbit.

wrong.why: thinks gravity ends outside the atmosphere
thinks gravity works only between planets

items.evidence: Mass is the constant amount of matter in a body, measured in kilograms, while weight is the force with which Earth pulls that body, measured in Newtons.
items.q: How is the mass of a body different from its weight?
options: Mass is amount of matter; weight is a pull
Mass is a pull; weight is amount of matter
Mass is weight; both are measured in kilograms
Mass changes with place; weight stays fixed
items.explain: Mass is the constant amount of matter; weight is the force with which Earth pulls.

wrong.why: swaps the meanings of mass and weight
thinks mass and weight are the same

items.evidence: Whether an object sinks or floats depends on the buoyant force relative to its weight, not just whether the object is heavy or light.
items.q: A heavy log floats but a light pebble sinks. What decides this?
options: Buoyant force compared with the object's weight
How heavy or light the object is
How much mass it loses when submerged
Water pressing only downwards on the object
items.explain: Sinking or floating depends on buoyant force relative to weight, not just heaviness.

wrong.why: thinks heavy objects sink and light ones float
thinks objects lose mass in water
